codeCard.title: Inheritance & Polymorphism in Action

checkpoint.question: What is the primary role of inheritance in Java object-oriented programming?
options: To establish an IS-A relationship allowing a subclass to reuse and specialize the accessible fields and methods of a superclass
To create multiple copies of a class on different JVM threads
To convert instance variables into static variables automatically
To encrypt class files before compilation
checkpoint.explanation: Inheritance models an IS-A relationship (e.g. Dog IS-A Animal) allowing a derived class (subclass) to inherit and build upon existing fields and methods of a parent class (superclass), maximizing code reuse.

checkpoint.question: Which Java keyword is used by a class to inherit from a superclass?
options: extends
implements
inherits
super
checkpoint.explanation: In Java, the 'extends' keyword is used in a class declaration to establish inheritance from a single superclass (e.g. class Manager extends Employee).

checkpoint.question: Given: class Parent { void show() { System.out.println("Parent show"); } } class Child extends Parent {} What does new Child().show() output?
options: Parent show
Child show
null
Compilation error because Child does not define show()
checkpoint.explanation: Child inherits all accessible methods from Parent. Since Child does not override show(), calling c.show() executes Parent's inherited show() method and outputs 'Parent show'.

codeCard.title: Using the super Keyword

checkpoint.question: What are the two primary uses of the 'super' keyword in Java?
options: To invoke a superclass constructor (super()) and to access shadowed superclass members or overridden methods (super.member)
To make a method run with elevated operating system permissions
To allocate memory on the JVM Metaspace directly
To define a class that cannot be inherited
checkpoint.explanation: 'super' refers to the immediate parent class. It is used as super(...) to call superclass constructors, or super.method() / super.field to access parent members shadowed or overridden in the subclass.

codeCard.title: Method Overriding Demonstration

checkpoint.question: What must be true for a subclass method to successfully override a superclass method in Java?
options: It must have the exact same method name, identical parameter list, and a compatible return type (covariant return type)
It must have different parameter types
It must have a private access modifier
It must return void regardless of what the parent returns
checkpoint.explanation: Method overriding requires identical method signatures (name + parameter types in order) and the return type must be identical or a subtype (covariant). The access modifier cannot be more restrictive.

codeCard.title: Final Method Overriding Prohibition

checkpoint.question: What occurs if a subclass attempts to override a method declared as 'final' in its superclass?
options: A compilation error occurs: 'cannot override final method from superclass'
The code compiles, but throws an IllegalAccessException at runtime
The final modifier is silently removed from the parent class
The method is executed using recursion
checkpoint.explanation: In Java, declaring a method as 'final' prevents subclasses from altering its behavior. Any attempt to override a final method results in a compile-time error.

callout.title: Engineering Principle
callout.text: Understanding Method Overloading Basics in OOPs continued - Inheritance, polymorphism is vital for architectural correctness and optimal performance.

codeCard.title: Compile-Time Polymorphism (Method Overloading)

checkpoint.question: Why is method overloading referred to as 'compile-time' (or static) polymorphism?
options: Because the compiler resolves exactly which overloaded method to execute at compile time based on the static reference types and count of the arguments
Because overloaded methods run during compilation and not during runtime
Because overloaded methods can only be written inside static blocks
Because the bytecode is translated into C code
checkpoint.explanation: Method overloading is resolved at compile time: javac inspects the argument types provided in the method call and chooses the most specific matching method signature.

pages.title: Choose the Correct Code

callout.title: Engineering Principle
callout.text: Understanding Choose the Correct Code in OOPs continued - Inheritance, polymorphism is vital for architectural correctness and optimal performance.

codeCard.title: Valid Overloading vs Invalid Overloading

checkpoint.question: Can two methods in the same class have the exact same name and parameter list, but differ only in their return type? Why or why not?
options: No, the Java compiler raises an error because return type alone is not part of the method signature used for overload resolution
Yes, the compiler determines which method to call based on how the caller assigns the return value
Yes, but only if one method is static and the other is non-static
Yes, if both methods are declared public
checkpoint.explanation: In Java, a method signature consists solely of the method name and the parameter types. The return type is NOT part of the method signature, so two methods with the same parameters but different return types cause a compile error.

practiceProblems.description:
You are given a partially written Java program that uses **inheritance** to represent different types of laptops.

There is a parent class called `Laptop` which contains a method `laptopInfo()` that prints a general message about laptops. You need to create two child classes: `GamingLaptop` and `BusinessLaptop`, each with their own unique method.

**Tasks:**

1. Create a class `Laptop` with a method:
 ```java
 void laptopInfo() {
 System.out.println("This is a general laptop");
 }
 ```

2. Create a class `GamingLaptop` that extends `Laptop` and includes a method:
 ```java
 void gamingFeatures() {
 System.out.println("Gaming Laptop has high-end graphics");
 }
 ```

3. Create a class `BusinessLaptop` that extends `Laptop` and includes a method:
 ```java
 void businessFeatures() {
 System.out.println("Business Laptop has long battery life");
 ```

4. In the `main()` method:
 - Create an object of `GamingLaptop` and call both `laptopInfo()` and `gamingFeatures()`
 - Create an object of `BusinessLaptop` and call both `laptopInfo()` and `businessFeatures()`

**Hint:**
Use the **extends** keyword to inherit from the `Laptop` class. You don’t need to use any constructors or input in this problem.

---

```java
This is a general laptop
Gaming Laptop has high-end graphics
This is a general laptop
Business Laptop has long battery life
```

topics.description: Study concepts and solve targeted engineering problems for Inheritance in Java.

pages.title: Inheritance in Java
pages.content:
Inheritance lets a subclass reuse accessible members of a superclass. Java class inheritance uses `extends`, and each class has one direct superclass.

Inheritance is most useful when the child truly represents a specialized form of the parent. Reused state or behavior should still remain appropriately encapsulated.

callout.title: Key Concept
callout.text: Inheritance in Java explains a Java design rule used in Inheritance in Java.

codeCard.code: class Person { String name="Asha"; } class Student extends Person {} public class Main { public static void main(String[] a){System.out.println(new Student().name);}}

checkpoint.question: In Java's inheritance model, which accessible members are inherited by a subclass from its superclass?
options: Public and protected fields and methods, as well as package-private members if both classes reside in the same package (constructors and private members are not inherited)
All members including private fields and constructors
Only static methods and constants
Only methods annotated with @Inherited
checkpoint.explanation: A subclass inherits all public and protected members of its superclass, plus default (package-private) members if in the same package. Private members and constructors are NOT inherited.

pages.title: Constructor Call Order
pages.content:
When an object of a subclass is created, the superclass constructor runs before the subclass constructor. A no-argument `super()` call is inserted when appropriate.

This ordering ensures that inherited state is initialized before subclass-specific initialization begins.

callout.title: Key Concept
callout.text: Constructor Call Order explains a Java design rule used in Inheritance in Java.

codeCard.code: class A { A(){System.out.println("A");} } class B extends A { B(){System.out.println("B");} } public class Main { public static void main(String[] a){new B();}}

checkpoint.question: When instantiating a subclass object (e.g. new Dog()), what is the guaranteed order of constructor execution?
options: Superclass constructor executes first, followed by the subclass constructor
Subclass constructor executes first, followed by the superclass constructor
Only the subclass constructor executes; superclass constructors do not run
The execution order is random depending on JVM thread priority
checkpoint.explanation: Superclass constructors always execute before subclass constructor bodies. This ensures that the foundational superclass state is initialized before specialized subclass code runs.

pages.title: Calling Superclass Constructor
pages.content:
A subclass constructor can explicitly call a superclass constructor with `super(...)`. The `super(...)` call must be the first statement in the constructor.

This is useful when the parent class requires parameters to initialize its own state.

callout.title: Key Concept
callout.text: Calling Superclass Constructor explains a Java design rule used in Inheritance in Java.

codeCard.code: class Person { String name; Person(String n){name=n;} } class Student extends Person { Student(String n){super(n);} } public class Main { public static void main(String[] a){System.out.println(new Student("Anu").name);}}

checkpoint.question: If a superclass defines ONLY a parameterized constructor (e.g. Super(int x)) and NO no-argument constructor, what MUST the subclass constructor do?
options: It must explicitly call super(x) as the first statement in its constructor
It can do nothing; the compiler will supply a 0 automatically
It must declare itself abstract
It must override the superclass constructor
checkpoint.explanation: If the superclass lacks a no-arg constructor, the compiler's implicit super() call fails. The subclass must explicitly invoke super(arguments) matching an available superclass constructor as its first statement.

pages.title: Step-by-step learning path
pages.content: Follow this exact sequence for **Inheritance in Java**: prerequisite check → concept build → mental model → worked example → dry run → guided implementation → independent practice → mastery gate. Do not skip to the final practice set until the guided implementation is understood.
pages.teachingGoal: Learner can complete step-by-step learning path for Inheritance in Java.

checkpoint.question: Why does the inheritance learning path emphasize modeling 'is-a' relationships strictly?
options: Because improper inheritance (using extends for mere code sharing) produces fragile base classes and violates the Liskov Substitution Principle
Because the Java compiler limits inheritance to 2 classes total
Because inheritance requires 64GB of RAM
Because subclasses cannot have instance variables
checkpoint.explanation: Inheritance is a structural commitment that a subclass IS-A superclass. Violating this (e.g. making Stack extend Vector) leads to leaked methods and broken invariants.

pages.title: 1. Prerequisite check
pages.content: Before starting **Inheritance in Java**, recall the Java syntax and object/model concepts required for it. Write down what you already know, then identify one question you cannot yet answer confidently. The purpose of this step is to expose a missing prerequisite before new material is introduced.
pages.teachingGoal: Learner can complete 1. prerequisite check for Inheritance in Java.

checkpoint.question: What is the root superclass of every class in Java, whether explicitly declared or not?
options: java.lang.Object
java.lang.Class
java.lang.System
java.lang.Root
checkpoint.explanation: Every class in Java implicitly inherits directly or indirectly from java.lang.Object, providing universal methods like equals(), hashCode(), toString(), and getClass().

pages.title: 2. Build the concept
pages.content: Inheritance expresses an is-a relationship. A subclass automatically receives accessible members from its superclass and may specialize behavior. Prefer inheritance when substitutability is meaningful; use composition when the relationship is has-a. Start with the rule, then connect the rule to one small Java example. Avoid memorizing a code template before you can explain why each important line is present.
pages.teachingGoal: Learner can complete 2. build the concept for Inheritance in Java.

checkpoint.question: What does the 'protected' access modifier permit in Java inheritance?
options: Access from any class within the same package, plus access from subclasses located in ANY package
Access only from subclasses in the same package
Access from all classes in the entire JVM without restriction
Access strictly within the declaring class body only
checkpoint.explanation: 'protected' members are package-private plus accessible to subclasses anywhere, allowing derived classes in different packages to access parent fields and helper methods.

pages.title: 3. Build a mental model
pages.content: Imagine the runtime state while **Inheritance in Java** executes. Identify the important actors, ownership, values, references, control flow, or exception paths. Explain the relationship in plain language before touching a full program.
pages.teachingGoal: Learner can complete 3. build a mental model for Inheritance in Java.

checkpoint.question: When visualizing an object of a subclass in heap memory, how are inherited superclass fields stored?
options: The single heap object contains memory slots for both superclass fields and subclass fields combined in one contiguous block
Two separate objects are created on the heap and linked via a network socket
Superclass fields are stored on the stack, and subclass fields are on the heap
Inherited fields are stored on disk
checkpoint.explanation: A subclass instance is a single object in the heap whose memory footprint includes slots for its own declared instance variables as well as all inherited superclass instance variables.

pages.title: 4. Worked example
pages.content: Take one small example for **Inheritance in Java** and solve it in visible steps: state the input, apply the first rule, update the state, and predict the output or effect. Then compare your reasoning with the executable example in this topic.
pages.teachingGoal: Learner can complete 4. worked example for Inheritance in Java.

checkpoint.question: Given: class A { A() { System.out.print("A"); } } class B extends A { B() { System.out.print("B"); } } What does new B() print?
options: "AB"
"BA"
checkpoint.explanation: new B() invokes constructor B(). The compiler inserts super() as the first statement, which calls constructor A() printing 'A'. Then constructor B() completes, printing 'B', producing 'AB'.

pages.title: 5. Dry run before execution
pages.content: Trace the program line by line using a state table. Record changed variables, object fields, references, collections, thread state, or exception flow. The goal is to make the execution predictable rather than mysterious.
pages.teachingGoal: Learner can complete 5. dry run before execution for Inheritance in Java.

checkpoint.question: What happens if super(...) is placed as the second statement inside a subclass constructor?
options: A compilation error occurs: 'call to super must be first statement in constructor'
The superclass constructor executes twice
The subclass constructor aborts silently
The JVM re-orders statements automatically
checkpoint.explanation: The Java compiler strictly enforces that any explicit super(...) or this(...) call must be the very first statement in a constructor body.

pages.title: 6. Guided implementation
pages.content: Implement a minimal version of **Inheritance in Java** using the starter structure supplied in the practice problem. First fill in the missing concept, then run the smallest sample, then expand to a second case. Do not optimize before the behavior is correct.
pages.teachingGoal: Learner can complete 6. guided implementation for Inheritance in Java.

checkpoint.question: How can a subclass access an instance field in its superclass that has been shadowed by a subclass field with the same name?
options: Using the super keyword (e.g. super.fieldName)
Using this.fieldName
Shadowed fields cannot be accessed under any circumstances
By casting the subclass to Object
checkpoint.explanation: If a subclass declares a field with the same name as an inherited superclass field, the subclass field shadows the parent field. 'super.fieldName' explicitly accesses the superclass field.

pages.title: 7. Independent practice
pages.content: Solve the **Inheritance in Java** practice problems in increasing difficulty. For every failure, classify it as syntax, concept, state-tracing, edge-case, or design error before changing the code.
pages.teachingGoal: Learner can complete 7. independent practice for Inheritance in Java.

checkpoint.question: Can a Java class extend multiple classes simultaneously (e.g. class C extends A, B)?
options: No, Java does not support multiple inheritance of classes to prevent ambiguity (Diamond Problem); a class can only extend one class
Yes, using commas to separate superclass names
Yes, if both superclasses are abstract
Yes, if both superclasses have no fields
checkpoint.explanation: Java disallows multiple class inheritance to eliminate diamond inheritance ambiguities. Multiple inheritance is achieved safely through interfaces.

pages.title: 8. Mastery gate
pages.content: You have mastered **Inheritance in Java** when you can: (1) explain the rule without notes, (2) dry-run a new example, (3) implement a small variation, (4) explain one common failure, and (5) choose when the concept should and should not be used.
pages.teachingGoal: Learner can complete 8. mastery gate for Inheritance in Java.

checkpoint.question: What is the effect of declaring a class as 'final' (e.g. public final class String)?
options: The class cannot be subclassed (extended) by any other class
All methods in the class become static
The class cannot be instantiated with new
All fields in the class become mutable
checkpoint.explanation: A final class cannot be extended. This is commonly used for security, immutability, and API stability (such as java.lang.String, Integer, and Math).

pages.title: 9. Debugging and misconception clinic
pages.content:
Use the following diagnostic routine:

- **Mistake:** Memorizing Inheritance in Java syntax without understanding its runtime behavior. 
  **Recovery:** return to the smallest example, state the governing rule, and rerun one change at a time.
- **Mistake:** Skipping prerequisite concepts and guessing from compiler errors alone. 
  **Recovery:** return to the smallest example, state the governing rule, and rerun one change at a time.
- **Mistake:** Testing only the sample input. 
  **Recovery:** return to the smallest example, state the governing rule, and rerun one change at a time.
- **Mistake:** Changing several parts of the program before identifying the failing concept. 
  **Recovery:** return to the smallest example, state the governing rule, and rerun one change at a time.
pages.teachingGoal: Diagnose common errors while learning Inheritance in Java.

checkpoint.question: What bug occurs when a superclass constructor invokes an overridable method that a subclass overrides to access subclass fields?
options: The overridden subclass method runs BEFORE the subclass constructor body has initialized its fields, reading default/uninitialized values (e.g. 0 or null)
The JVM throws a ClassCircularityError
The superclass constructor enters an infinite loop
The superclass fields are erased
checkpoint.explanation: Never invoke overridable methods inside constructors! When super() runs, subclass fields have not yet been initialized. Calling an overridden method executes the subclass method against uninitialized fields.

pages.title: 10. Mastery review and interview transfer
pages.content:
Finish **Inheritance in Java** by answering these without notes:

1. What problem does this concept solve?
2. What is the smallest correct example?
3. What invariant or rule must remain true?
4. What edge case commonly breaks naive solutions?
5. What is one interview question you could answer from this topic?

Then solve one unseen variation before marking the topic complete.
pages.teachingGoal: Transfer Inheritance in Java from guided learning to independent problem solving.

checkpoint.question: In an interview, how would you articulate the core trade-off of using inheritance?
options: Inheritance maximizes code reuse and polymorphism, but introduces tight coupling to superclass implementation details (fragile base class problem)
Inheritance is always faster than composition in bytecode execution
Inheritance replaces the need for unit testing
Inheritance allows variables to bypass garbage collection
checkpoint.explanation: Inheritance creates a tight compile-time coupling where subclasses depend heavily on base class internals. It should only be used when a strict IS-A relationship holds.

topics.title: Polymorphism in Java
topics.description: Study concepts and solve targeted engineering problems for Polymorphism in Java.

pages.title: Polymorphism in Java
pages.content:
Polymorphism lets one interface or parent type represent objects of different concrete classes. Java supports compile-time polymorphism through method overloading and runtime polymorphism through method overriding.

The declared type controls which members are visible, while runtime dispatch selects an overridden instance method implementation.

callout.title: Key Concept
callout.text: Polymorphism in Java explains a Java design rule used in Polymorphism in Java.

codeCard.code: class Shape { String draw(){return "Shape";} } class Circle extends Shape { String draw(){return "Circle";} } public class Main { public static void main(String[] a){Shape s=new Circle();System.out.println(s.draw());}}

checkpoint.question: What does the term 'Polymorphism' literally mean and how is it realized in Java?
options: Literally 'many forms': the ability of a single interface or parent reference to take on different behaviors depending on the actual underlying object instance
The ability to run Java bytecode on multiple operating systems
The process of converting Java source code into bytecode
Having multiple classes inside a single .java source file
checkpoint.explanation: Polymorphism means 'many forms'. In Java, it allows a reference of a supertype to refer to objects of different subtypes, invoking overridden methods dynamically.

pages.title: Function Overloading
pages.content:
Method overloading defines multiple methods with the same name but different parameter lists. The compiler chooses the matching overload from the argument types and count.

Changing only the return type is not enough to overload a method.

callout.title: Key Concept
callout.text: Function Overloading explains a Java design rule used in Polymorphism in Java.

codeCard.code: class Calc { int add(int a,int b){return a+b;} int add(int a,int b,int c){return a+b+c;} } public class Main { public static void main(String[] a){Calc c=new Calc();System.out.println(c.add(2,3,4));}}

checkpoint.question: In method overloading, what criteria does the compiler examine to differentiate between overloaded methods?
options: The method name must be the same, but the number, data types, or sequence of parameters must differ
The return type must be different
The access modifier must be different
The method names must have different numbers of letters
checkpoint.explanation: Overloading requires distinct parameter lists (signatures) within the same class. Return types, access modifiers, or exception clauses alone do not distinguish overloads.

pages.title: Multiple Choice Question
pages.content:
This page reinforces the surrounding topic with a focused concept check. Pay attention to what belongs to the class, what belongs to an object, and what the Java compiler requires.

Read the example carefully before answering: the goal is to connect the syntax to the runtime behavior it produces.

callout.title: Key Concept
callout.text: Multiple Choice Question explains a Java design rule used in Polymorphism in Java.

codeCard.title: Method Overloading by Parameter Type Order

checkpoint.question: Consider: void calculate(int a, double b) {} and void calculate(double a, int b) {} Is this valid method overloading in Java?
options: Yes, because the order of parameter types (int, double vs double, int) is distinct
No, because both methods use int and double
No, because return types are both void
No, because parameter names are identical
checkpoint.explanation: Overloading considers the sequence of parameter types. (int, double) is a distinct parameter signature from (double, int), making it a valid overload.

pages.title: Java Constructor Overloading
pages.content:
Constructors can also be overloaded. A class may provide several constructors with different parameter lists so callers can create objects with different initialization options.

Each constructor should establish a valid object state and avoid unnecessary duplicated initialization logic.

callout.title: Key Concept
callout.text: Java Constructor Overloading explains a Java design rule used in Polymorphism in Java.

codeCard.code: class Box { int x; Box(){x=0;} Box(int v){x=v;} } public class Main { public static void main(String[] a){System.out.println(new Box(8).x);}}

checkpoint.question: Why do classes like java.lang.String or java.util.ArrayList provide multiple overloaded constructors?
options: To give callers flexibility to initialize objects from different data sources (e.g. empty, char[], byte[], or initial capacity)
Because each constructor can only allocate 1KB of memory
Because Java requires a separate constructor for each instance created
To allow subclasses to inherit different versions
checkpoint.explanation: Constructor overloading provides multiple convenient initialization paths, allowing callers to construct objects from defaults, collections, arrays, or custom configuration parameters.

pages.title: Advantages of Function Overloading
pages.content:
Overloading provides a consistent operation name for related inputs. Callers can use the same method name while the compiler selects the appropriate parameter signature.

This can improve readability when the overloaded operations represent the same conceptual behavior.

callout.title: Key Concept
callout.text: Advantages of Function Overloading explains a Java design rule used in Polymorphism in Java.

codeCard.code: class Printer { void print(int x){System.out.println(x);} void print(String x){System.out.println(x);} } public class Main { public static void main(String[] a){Printer p=new Printer();p.print(5);p.print("Java");}}

checkpoint.question: What is a major software design advantage of method overloading in a public API?
options: It provides a clean, consistent naming convention across related operations (e.g. Math.max(int, int) and Math.max(double, double)) instead of awkward names like maxInt and maxDouble
It forces methods to run asynchronously in parallel threads
It eliminates the need for unit testing
It reduces memory usage in the JVM heap
checkpoint.explanation: Overloading avoids cluttering the API with distinct method names for identical logical operations on different data types (e.g. print(int), print(String) vs printInt, printString).

pages.title: Step-by-step learning path
pages.content: Follow this exact sequence for **Polymorphism in Java**: prerequisite check → concept build → mental model → worked example → dry run → guided implementation → independent practice → mastery gate. Do not skip to the final practice set until the guided implementation is understood.
pages.teachingGoal: Learner can complete step-by-step learning path for Polymorphism in Java.

checkpoint.question: What are the two distinct types of polymorphism in Java?
options: Compile-time polymorphism (Method Overloading) and Runtime polymorphism (Method Overriding via dynamic dispatch)
Static polymorphism and Dynamic memory allocation
Stack polymorphism and Heap polymorphism
Class polymorphism and Package polymorphism
checkpoint.explanation: Java features compile-time (static) polymorphism achieved through method overloading, and runtime (dynamic) polymorphism achieved through method overriding and upcasting.

pages.title: 1. Prerequisite check
pages.content: Before starting **Polymorphism in Java**, recall the Java syntax and object/model concepts required for it. Write down what you already know, then identify one question you cannot yet answer confidently. The purpose of this step is to expose a missing prerequisite before new material is introduced.
pages.teachingGoal: Learner can complete 1. prerequisite check for Polymorphism in Java.

checkpoint.question: In method overload resolution, what does the Java compiler do when exact parameter type matches are unavailable?
options: It performs automatic type promotion (e.g. byte -> short -> int -> long -> float -> double) to find the closest compatible method
It immediately throws an IllegalArgumentException
It deletes the method call from bytecode
It generates a new method at runtime
checkpoint.explanation: If an exact type match is not found, javac applies primitive widening/type promotion (e.g. an int argument will match a double parameter if no int overload exists).

pages.title: 2. Build the concept
pages.content: Polymorphism lets code depend on a common type while the runtime object determines overridden behavior. The useful mental model is 'reference type controls what members are visible; runtime type controls overridden implementation dispatch.' Start with the rule, then connect the rule to one small Java example. Avoid memorizing a code template before you can explain why each important line is present.
pages.teachingGoal: Learner can complete 2. build the concept for Polymorphism in Java.

checkpoint.question: What occurs during method overload resolution if the compiler finds two equally specific methods (e.g. method(int, double) and method(double, int) called with (10, 20))?
options: A compilation error occurs: 'reference to method is ambiguous'
The compiler picks the first method defined in the source file
The JVM picks one randomly at runtime
Both methods execute sequentially
checkpoint.explanation: If two overloaded methods can both accept the arguments via type promotion without one being strictly more specific than the other, javac flags an ambiguity error.

pages.title: 3. Build a mental model
pages.content: Imagine the runtime state while **Polymorphism in Java** executes. Identify the important actors, ownership, values, references, control flow, or exception paths. Explain the relationship in plain language before touching a full program.
pages.teachingGoal: Learner can complete 3. build a mental model for Polymorphism in Java.

checkpoint.question: In the JVM specification, which bytecode instruction is used to invoke overloaded methods resolved at compile time versus overridden instance methods?
options: invokestatic / invokespecial for static/private methods vs invokevirtual / invokeinterface for polymorphic instance methods
invokemany vs invokeone
call vs jump
exec_stack vs exec_heap
checkpoint.explanation: Compile-time resolved methods use invokestatic or invokespecial. Polymorphic instance methods use invokevirtual (or invokeinterface), which look up the method table of the actual runtime object.

pages.title: 4. Worked example
pages.content: Take one small example for **Polymorphism in Java** and solve it in visible steps: state the input, apply the first rule, update the state, and predict the output or effect. Then compare your reasoning with the executable example in this topic.
pages.teachingGoal: Learner can complete 4. worked example for Polymorphism in Java.

checkpoint.question: Given: class Calculator { int add(int a, int b) { return a+b; } double add(double a, double b) { return a+b; } } What does calc.add(5, 10.5) invoke?
options: add(double, double), because integer 5 is widened to 5.0 to match the double parameter
add(int, int)
Compilation error: cannot mix int and double
It creates a new add(int, double) method automatically
checkpoint.explanation: Parameter 5 is an int and 10.5 is a double. To match add(double, double), int 5 is widened to double 5.0, cleanly matching the method.

pages.title: 5. Dry run before execution
pages.content: Trace the program line by line using a state table. Record changed variables, object fields, references, collections, thread state, or exception flow. The goal is to make the execution predictable rather than mysterious.
pages.teachingGoal: Learner can complete 5. dry run before execution for Polymorphism in Java.

checkpoint.question: What happens when resolving overloads with autoboxing and varargs: void test(int x) and void test(Integer x)? Called with test(5):
options: test(int x) is invoked because primitive matching has higher priority than autoboxing to Integer
test(Integer x) is invoked because objects have priority
Ambiguity compile error
Both methods run
checkpoint.explanation: Java overload resolution order prioritizes: (1) Exact match without conversion, (2) Widening primitive, (3) Autoboxing/unboxing, (4) Varargs. Exact primitive int beats autoboxed Integer.

pages.title: 6. Guided implementation
pages.content: Implement a minimal version of **Polymorphism in Java** using the starter structure supplied in the practice problem. First fill in the missing concept, then run the smallest sample, then expand to a second case. Do not optimize before the behavior is correct.
pages.teachingGoal: Learner can complete 6. guided implementation for Polymorphism in Java.

checkpoint.question: How can variable-length argument lists (varargs: Type... args) be used in method overloading?
options: Varargs can be overloaded, but the varargs method is always treated as the lowest-priority fallback match by the compiler
Varargs cannot be used in overloaded methods
Varargs methods always take precedence over exact matches
Varargs methods must have return type void
checkpoint.explanation: Varargs (introduced in Java 5) can be overloaded, but javac treats varargs as the last resort fallback if no fixed-arity method matches.

pages.title: 7. Independent practice
pages.content: Solve the **Polymorphism in Java** practice problems in increasing difficulty. For every failure, classify it as syntax, concept, state-tracing, edge-case, or design error before changing the code.
pages.teachingGoal: Learner can complete 7. independent practice for Polymorphism in Java.

checkpoint.question: Why should developers avoid excessive or tricky method overloading involving similar primitive types or inheritance hierarchies?
options: It can confuse callers and lead to unexpected method selection due to complex promotion or autoboxing rules
It crashes the javac compiler
It causes memory leaks in Metaspace
It makes the class incompatible with JSON serialization
checkpoint.explanation: Overloading methods with similar or easily-convertible types (e.g. List.remove(int index) vs List.remove(Object o)) causes notorious bugs when callers pass integers expecting object removal.

pages.title: 8. Mastery gate
pages.content: You have mastered **Polymorphism in Java** when you can: (1) explain the rule without notes, (2) dry-run a new example, (3) implement a small variation, (4) explain one common failure, and (5) choose when the concept should and should not be used.
pages.teachingGoal: Learner can complete 8. mastery gate for Polymorphism in Java.

checkpoint.question: What is the critical distinction in how Java handles method overloading vs method overriding?
options: Overloading is resolved at compile time based on parameter types (same class); Overriding is resolved at runtime based on the actual object type (subclass hierarchy)
Overloading uses extends; Overriding uses implements
Overloading is for static methods only; Overriding is for private methods only
There is no difference between overloading and overriding
checkpoint.explanation: Overloading = same method name, different parameters, resolved at compile-time within a class. Overriding = same method name and signature, redefined in a subclass, resolved at runtime.

Use the following diagnostic routine:

- **Mistake:** Memorizing Polymorphism in Java syntax without understanding its runtime behavior. 
  **Recovery:** return to the smallest example, state the governing rule, and rerun one change at a time.
- **Mistake:** Skipping prerequisite concepts and guessing from compiler errors alone. 
  **Recovery:** return to the smallest example, state the governing rule, and rerun one change at a time.
- **Mistake:** Testing only the sample input. 
  **Recovery:** return to the smallest example, state the governing rule, and rerun one change at a time.
- **Mistake:** Changing several parts of the program before identifying the failing concept. 
  **Recovery:** return to the smallest example, state the governing rule, and rerun one change at a time.
pages.teachingGoal: Diagnose common errors while learning Polymorphism in Java.

checkpoint.question: In List<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>(List.of(1, 2, 3)); what does list.remove(1) do?
options: It calls remove(int index), removing the element at index 1 (which is 2), NOT the value 1!
It removes the value 1 from the list
It throws an IndexOutOfBoundsException
It clears the entire list
checkpoint.explanation: Because of primitive overload preference, list.remove(1) matches remove(int index) rather than remove(Object o). To remove the integer value 1, you must write list.remove(Integer.valueOf(1)).

topics.description: Study concepts and solve targeted engineering problems for Method overriding in Java.

pages.title: Method Overriding
pages.content:
Overriding occurs when a subclass provides a new implementation of an inherited instance method with a compatible signature.

Using `@Override` lets the compiler verify that the method actually overrides a superclass method.

callout.title: Key Concept
callout.text: Method Overriding explains a Java design rule used in Method overriding in Java.

codeCard.code: class A { String get(){return "A";} } class B extends A { String get(){return "B";} } public class Main { public static void main(String[] a){System.out.println(new B().get());}}

checkpoint.question: What is method overriding in Java?
options: A subclass providing a specific implementation of an instance method that is already defined by its superclass with an identical signature
Defining multiple methods with the same name but different parameters in the same class
Declaring a method as private in both superclass and subclass
Hiding a static method using another static method
checkpoint.explanation: Method overriding enables runtime polymorphism: a subclass provides its own specialized implementation of a method declared in its superclass, keeping the same name and parameter signature.

pages.title: How to override methods in Java
pages.content:
To override a method, keep the same method name and compatible parameter list in the subclass. The return type must be compatible, and visibility cannot be reduced.

The `@Override` annotation is recommended because it catches common signature mistakes during compilation.

callout.title: Key Concept
callout.text: How to override methods in Java explains a Java design rule used in Method overriding in Java.

codeCard.code: class Animal { void sound(){System.out.println("sound");} } class Dog extends Animal { @Override void sound(){System.out.println("bark");} } public class Main { public static void main(String[] a){new Dog().sound();}}

checkpoint.question: What is a 'covariant return type' in Java method overriding?
options: An overriding method in a subclass can declare a return type that is a subtype (subclass) of the return type declared in the superclass method
The return type must be void in the subclass
The return type must be a primitive integer
The return type must change on every execution
checkpoint.explanation: Since Java 5, an overriding method may return a more specific subtype of the superclass method's return type (e.g. superclass returns Animal, subclass returns Dog). This is known as a covariant return type.

pages.title: Overriding Final Method
pages.content:
A method declared `final` cannot be overridden by a subclass. This is useful when a class must guarantee one implementation for a particular operation.

A subclass can still define a different method with a different signature, but that is overloading or a separate method, not overriding.

callout.title: Key Concept
callout.text: Overriding Final Method explains a Java design rule used in Method overriding in Java.

codeCard.code: class Base { final void show(){System.out.println("base");} } public class Main { public static void main(String[] a){new Base().show();}}

checkpoint.question: Can a subclass override a method declared as 'public final void lock()' in its superclass?
options: No, the final modifier prevents the method from being overridden; doing so causes a compile-time error
Yes, but only if the subclass is also marked final
Yes, if the subclass removes the final modifier
Yes, if the method is invoked using super.lock()
checkpoint.explanation: A method declared 'final' cannot be overridden by any subclass. It locks down the implementation to ensure security, predictability, and prevent behavior alteration.

pages.title: Method Overriding Access Modifiers
pages.content:
An overriding method may keep or widen visibility, but it cannot reduce the superclass method's accessibility.

For example, a `protected` method can be overridden as `protected` or `public`, but not as `private`.

callout.title: Key Concept
callout.text: Method Overriding Access Modifiers explains a Java design rule used in Method overriding in Java.

codeCard.code: class Base { protected void show(){System.out.println("base");} } class Child extends Base { @Override public void show(){System.out.println("child");} } public class Main { public static void main(String[] a){new Child().show();}}

checkpoint.question: If a superclass method has 'protected' visibility, what access modifier can the overriding subclass method use?
options: protected or public (visibility can be maintained or widened, but NEVER narrowed to default or private)
private only
default (package-private) only
Only final
checkpoint.explanation: An overriding method cannot assign weaker access privileges than the superclass method (LSP). If the parent is protected, the child can be protected or public, but not default or private.

pages.title: Method Overriding Requirements in Java
pages.content:
For true overriding, the subclass method must match the inherited instance method's signature and obey Java's access and exception rules.

Static methods are hidden rather than overridden, and constructors are never overridden.

callout.title: Key Concept
callout.text: Method Overriding Requirements in Java explains a Java design rule used in Method overriding in Java.

codeCard.code: class Base { void show(){System.out.println("base");} } class Child extends Base { @Override void show(){System.out.println("child");} } public class Main { public static void main(String[] a){Base b=new Child();b.show();}}

checkpoint.question: Regarding checked exceptions, what rule must an overriding method follow in Java?
options: It can throw fewer exceptions or narrower subclass exceptions, but CANNOT declare new or broader checked exceptions than the superclass method
It must declare at least five checked exceptions
It must throw java.lang.Exception in all cases
It cannot catch any exceptions inside its body
checkpoint.explanation: An overriding method cannot declare new or broader checked exceptions than those declared by the superclass method, ensuring callers expecting the supertype contract are never surprised.

pages.title: Step-by-step learning path
pages.content: Follow this exact sequence for **Method overriding in Java**: prerequisite check → concept build → mental model → worked example → dry run → guided implementation → independent practice → mastery gate. Do not skip to the final practice set until the guided implementation is understood.
pages.teachingGoal: Learner can complete step-by-step learning path for Method overriding in Java.

checkpoint.question: Why should developers always annotate overriding methods with @Override?
options: It instructs the compiler to verify that the method actually overrides a supertype method, catching accidental typos and signature mismatches
It speeds up bytecode execution by 20%
It is required by the JVM class verifier
It makes private methods visible to subclasses
checkpoint.explanation: @Override causes a compiler error if the method does not actually match a superclass/interface method, immediately exposing subtle bugs like typing equals(MyClass) instead of equals(Object).

pages.title: 1. Prerequisite check
pages.content: Before starting **Method overriding in Java**, recall the Java syntax and object/model concepts required for it. checkpoint.question: Can private methods of a superclass be overridden by a subclass?
options: No, private methods are invisible to subclasses and therefore cannot be overridden; declaring the same method in a subclass is considered an unrelated new method
Yes, private methods are overridden automatically
Yes, using the @Override annotation
Yes, if both classes are in the same package
checkpoint.explanation: Private methods are bound statically to the declaring class and are inaccessible outside it. A subclass declaring a method with the same signature merely defines an independent method, not an override.

pages.title: 2. Build the concept
pages.content: Overriding replaces inherited instance behavior in a subclass. The signature must match the inherited method according to Java's overriding rules, and access cannot be reduced. Use @Override so the compiler catches accidental signature mismatches. Start with the rule, then connect the rule to one small Java example. Avoid memorizing a code template before you can explain why each important line is present.
pages.teachingGoal: Learner can complete 2. build the concept for Method overriding in Java.

checkpoint.question: Can static methods in Java be overridden with polymorphic dynamic dispatch?
options: No, static methods cannot be overridden; redefining a static method in a subclass merely 'hides' the superclass method based on compile-time reference type
Yes, static methods participate in runtime dynamic dispatch
Yes, but only if they are declared public
Yes, if invoked through an interface
checkpoint.explanation: Static methods belong to the class, not individual objects. They are resolved at compile time based on reference type (Method Hiding), never via runtime dynamic dispatch.

pages.title: 3. Build a mental model
pages.content: Imagine the runtime state while **Method overriding in Java** executes. Identify the important actors, ownership, values, references, control flow, or exception paths. Explain the relationship in plain language before touching a full program.
pages.teachingGoal: Learner can complete 3. build a mental model for Method overriding in Java.

checkpoint.question: What runtime data structure does the JVM use to look up overridden instance methods during dynamic method dispatch?
options: The Virtual Method Table (vtable) associated with the actual runtime class of the object
The thread call stack frame pointer
The Metaspace garbage collector registry
A hash map of string method names loaded from disk
checkpoint.explanation: The JVM maintains a virtual method table (vtable) for each class containing pointers to the executable code of its instance methods. Invoking an overridden method queries this table at runtime.

pages.title: 4. Worked example
pages.content: Take one small example for **Method overriding in Java** and solve it in visible steps: state the input, apply the first rule, update the state, and predict the output or effect. Then compare your reasoning with the executable example in this topic.
pages.teachingGoal: Learner can complete 4. worked example for Method overriding in Java.

checkpoint.question: Given: class Animal { void speak() { System.out.print("Animal "); } } class Cat extends Animal { void speak() { super.speak(); System.out.print("Meow"); } } What does new Cat().speak() output?
options: "Animal Meow"
"Meow Animal"
"Meow"
"Animal "
checkpoint.explanation: Cat's speak() method first calls super.speak(), which prints 'Animal '. Then it prints 'Meow', resulting in 'Animal Meow'.

pages.title: 5. Dry run before execution
pages.content: Trace the program line by line using a state table. Record changed variables, object fields, references, collections, thread state, or exception flow. The goal is to make the execution predictable rather than mysterious.
pages.teachingGoal: Learner can complete 5. dry run before execution for Method overriding in Java.

checkpoint.question: Given: Animal a = new Cat(); a.speak(); In this statement, which type determines whether speak() is a valid method call at COMPILE time, and which determines what executes at RUNTIME?
options: Compile-time validity is checked against reference type Animal; Runtime execution is dispatched to actual object type Cat
Both compile-time and runtime are checked against Animal
Both compile-time and runtime are checked against Cat
Compile time is Cat; runtime is Animal
checkpoint.explanation: The compiler checks that the method exists on the declared reference type (Animal). At runtime, the JVM inspects the heap object (Cat) and executes Cat's overridden implementation.

pages.title: 6. Guided implementation
pages.content: Implement a minimal version of **Method overriding in Java** using the starter structure supplied in the practice problem. First fill in the missing concept, then run the smallest sample, then expand to a second case. Do not optimize before the behavior is correct.

checkpoint.question: If a subclass adds extra functionality inside an overridden method, how can it preserve the parent class's behavior?
options: By invoking super.methodName(args) within the overriding method body
By declaring the method static
By creating a new instance of the superclass
By catching a SuperclassException
checkpoint.explanation: Calling super.methodName(...) executes the base implementation, allowing the subclass to extend (rather than completely replace) the superclass's behavior.

pages.title: 7. Independent practice
pages.content: Solve the **Method overriding in Java** practice problems in increasing difficulty. For every failure, classify it as syntax, concept, state-tracing, edge-case, or design error before changing the code.

checkpoint.question: In an accounting system, class Account has calculateInterest(). CheckingAccount and SavingsAccount override it. If Account[] accounts contains both types, what happens when looping and calling a.calculateInterest()?
options: Each account calculates interest using its own specialized overridden logic automatically (polymorphic loop)
All accounts calculate interest using the generic Account logic
The program throws an ArrayStoreException
Only the first account in the array executes
checkpoint.explanation: Dynamic method dispatch ensures that each element in the array executes its specific overridden calculateInterest() method without needing instanceof checks or manual branching.

pages.title: 8. Mastery gate
pages.content: You have mastered **Method overriding in Java** when you can: (1) explain the rule without notes, (2) dry-run a new example, (3) implement a small variation, (4) explain one common failure, and (5) choose when the concept should and should not be used.

checkpoint.question: What is the difference between method hiding and method overriding in Java?
options: Method hiding applies to static methods (resolved at compile time); Method overriding applies to instance methods (resolved at runtime)
Method hiding uses the private keyword; Method overriding uses public
Method hiding is deprecated; Method overriding is new in Java 21
There is no difference
checkpoint.explanation: Static methods cannot be overridden; redefining a static method in a subclass hides the superclass version based on the compile-time reference type. Instance methods are overridden polymorphically.

pages.title: 9. Debugging and misconception clinic

Use the following diagnostic routine:

- **Mistake:** Memorizing Method overriding in Java syntax without understanding its runtime behavior.

- **Mistake:** Skipping prerequisite concepts and guessing from compiler errors alone.

- **Mistake:** Testing only the sample input. 
  **Recovery:** return to the smallest example, state the governing rule, and rerun one change at a time.
- **Mistake:** Changing several parts of the program before identifying the failing concept. 
  **Recovery:** return to the smallest example, state the governing rule, and rerun one change at a time.
pages.teachingGoal: Diagnose common errors while learning Method overriding in Java.

checkpoint.question: What mistake is made when a developer attempts to override boolean equals(Object o) by writing boolean equals(Person p)?
options: It overloads equals() instead of overriding it, so Collections like HashSet will continue calling Object.equals(Object), causing duplicate detection to fail
It causes a compilation error
It deletes the Person object from memory
It changes the return type to void
checkpoint.explanation: Writing equals(Person p) changes the parameter type from Object to Person, which creates an overload, not an override. Java Collections rely on equals(Object), so your method will never be called by collections!

checkpoint.question: In a technical interview, why is method overriding considered essential to the Open/Closed Principle (OCP)?
options: It allows extending system behavior by adding new subclasses that override methods, without modifying existing client code that calls those methods
It makes all methods final by default
It forces all classes to be stored in open-source repositories
It removes the need for object instantiation
checkpoint.explanation: OCP states software entities should be open for extension but closed for modification. Subclasses can override methods to add new behavior without touching or breaking existing code.

topics.description: Study concepts and solve targeted engineering problems for Interfaces & Abstract classes in Java.

pages.title: Interfaces in Java
pages.content:
An interface defines a contract that implementing classes must satisfy. A class uses `implements` and provides implementations for the interface's abstract methods unless the class itself is abstract.

A class can implement multiple interfaces, which is Java's standard mechanism for combining multiple contracts.

callout.title: Key Concept
callout.text: Interfaces in Java explains a Java design rule used in Interfaces & Abstract classes in Java.

codeCard.code: interface Printable { void print(); } class Report implements Printable { public void print(){System.out.println("report");} } public class Main { public static void main(String[] a){new Report().print();}}

checkpoint.question: What is an interface in Java?
options: A completely abstract blueprint defining a contract of methods that implementing classes must fulfill
A concrete class that can be instantiated with 'new'
A binary executable file compiled to C code
A private inner class
checkpoint.explanation: An interface defines a public contract of abstract behaviors (and default/static methods) that any implementing class promises to implement, decoupling specifications from implementations.

pages.title: How to use Interfaces in Java
pages.content:
Program to the interface type when possible. Store an implementation object in an interface reference so the caller depends on the contract rather than a concrete class.

This makes implementations replaceable and supports runtime polymorphism.

callout.title: Key Concept
callout.text: How to use Interfaces in Java explains a Java design rule used in Interfaces & Abstract classes in Java.

codeCard.code: interface Pay { int amount(); } class Cash implements Pay { public int amount(){return 100;} } public class Main { public static void main(String[] a){Pay p=new Cash();System.out.println(p.amount());}}

checkpoint.question: What is the industry best practice known as 'Programming to an Interface'?
options: Declaring variable and parameter types as the interface (e.g. List<String> list = new ArrayList<>()) rather than concrete implementation types
Writing interfaces without any implementing classes
Avoiding all classes and only using interfaces
Making all interfaces package-private
checkpoint.explanation: Programming to interfaces (e.g. List list = new ArrayList()) decouples client code from specific implementations, allowing the underlying implementation to be swapped with zero changes to caller code.

pages.title: Abstract Class
pages.content:
An abstract class cannot be instantiated directly. It can contain fields, constructors, concrete methods, and abstract methods.

A concrete subclass must implement the inherited abstract methods unless the subclass is also abstract.

callout.title: Key Concept
callout.text: Abstract Class explains a Java design rule used in Interfaces & Abstract classes in Java.

codeCard.code: abstract class Shape { abstract int area(); } class Square extends Shape { int x; Square(int x){this.x=x;} int area(){return x*x;} } public class Main { public static void main(String[] a){System.out.println(new Square(5).area());}}

checkpoint.question: Can an abstract class in Java be directly instantiated with the 'new' keyword?
options: No, abstract classes are incomplete by definition and cannot be directly instantiated; they must be extended by concrete subclasses
Yes, if all methods have default implementations
Yes, using the abstract new operator
Yes, if the class has a public constructor
checkpoint.explanation: The 'abstract' modifier tells the compiler that the class is an incomplete blueprint. Attempting to execute 'new AbstractClass()' results in a compile-time error.

pages.title: Purpose of Abstract Methods
pages.content:
An abstract method specifies behavior that subclasses must provide without supplying the implementation itself.

This allows the base class to define a common API while leaving subclass-specific behavior to concrete types.

callout.title: Key Concept
callout.text: Purpose of Abstract Methods explains a Java design rule used in Interfaces & Abstract classes in Java.

codeCard.code: abstract class Animal { abstract String sound(); } class Dog extends Animal { String sound(){return "bark";} } public class Main { public static void main(String[] a){System.out.println(new Dog().sound());}}

checkpoint.question: What is an abstract method in Java?
options: A method declared without a body (no curly braces, ending with a semicolon) that subclasses MUST implement
A method that runs in background threads
A method that takes no arguments and returns void
A method that can only be called once
checkpoint.explanation: An abstract method (e.g. abstract void draw();) defines the method signature and contract while leaving the concrete implementation to be provided by non-abstract subclasses.

pages.title: Abstract Class Constructors in Java
pages.content:
An abstract class can have constructors even though the class itself cannot be instantiated. The constructor runs as part of constructing a concrete subclass.

This is useful for initializing state shared by all subclasses.

callout.title: Key Concept
callout.text: Abstract Class Constructors in Java explains a Java design rule used in Interfaces & Abstract classes in Java.

codeCard.code: abstract class Base { Base(){System.out.println("base");} } class Child extends Base { } public class Main { public static void main(String[] a){new Child();}}

checkpoint.question: Can an abstract class have constructors if it cannot be instantiated directly with 'new'?
options: Yes, abstract classes can have constructors, which are invoked by subclass constructors via super() to initialize inherited fields
No, abstract classes cannot declare constructors under any circumstances
Yes, but they must be declared abstract
Yes, but they can only be called from static methods
checkpoint.explanation: Abstract classes frequently declare constructors to initialize shared state (e.g. name, id). When a concrete subclass is instantiated, its constructor invokes the abstract class constructor via super().

pages.title: Abstract Class Characteristics
pages.content:
Abstract classes support partial implementation and shared state. They are useful when related classes need common behavior as well as one or more required operations.

Use an abstract class when there is a meaningful common base implementation; use interfaces for contracts that may cut across unrelated class hierarchies.

callout.title: Key Concept
callout.text: Abstract Class Characteristics explains a Java design rule used in Interfaces & Abstract classes in Java.

codeCard.code: abstract class Vehicle { abstract String type(); } class Car extends Vehicle { String type(){return "car";} } public class Main { public static void main(String[] a){Vehicle v=new Car();System.out.println(v.type());}}

checkpoint.question: What is a primary difference between an abstract class and an interface in Java (prior to Java 8)?
options: An abstract class can hold mutable instance state (fields) and non-abstract methods, whereas an interface could only declare constants and abstract methods
An abstract class can be instantiated, while an interface cannot
A class can extend multiple abstract classes, but only implement one interface
Interfaces cannot be public
checkpoint.explanation: Abstract classes can maintain instance variables, constructors, and shared state across a class hierarchy. Interfaces define pure behavioral contracts and do not hold mutable instance fields.

checkpoint.question: When should you choose an Abstract Class over an Interface in Java architecture?
options: When related classes share common state (instance variables) and code implementation, or when you need non-public access modifiers (like protected)
When you need multiple inheritance of type across unrelated classes
When all methods must be static
Always, because interfaces are deprecated
checkpoint.explanation: Choose an abstract class when classes in a hierarchy share common non-static fields and core implementation logic. Choose interfaces when defining a role or contract across disparate, unrelated classes.

Multiple class inheritance
Destructors
Global functions
checkpoint.explanation: Java 8 introduced 'default' methods in interfaces, allowing interfaces to provide a default method body. Implementing classes inherit this implementation unless they choose to override it.

checkpoint.question: Can a single Java class implement multiple interfaces? Why is this allowed while multiple class inheritance is not?
options: Yes, a class can implement multiple interfaces because interfaces do not hold mutable instance state, avoiding state-related multiple inheritance conflicts
No, Java restricts classes to one interface only
Yes, but only if all interfaces are empty marker interfaces
No, multiple implementation was removed in Java 17
checkpoint.explanation: A class can implement any number of interfaces (e.g. class Task implements Runnable, Serializable, Comparable). Because interfaces declare contracts rather than object state, the Diamond Problem of state is avoided.

checkpoint.question: Given interface Flyable { void fly(); } and interface Swimmable { void swim(); } Which class header correctly implements both?

class Duck extends Flyable, Swimmable { }
class Duck implements Flyable extends Swimmable { }
class Duck uses Flyable & Swimmable { }

checkpoint.question: If class C implements interfaces A and B, and both A and B declare the exact same default method void log(), how does Java resolve the conflict?
options: The compiler flags an error, forcing class C to override log() and explicitly choose or implement its own behavior (e.g. A.super.log())
The compiler picks interface A automatically
The compiler picks interface B automatically
Both methods run sequentially
checkpoint.explanation: If a class inherits conflicting default methods from two interfaces, javac requires the implementing class to resolve the ambiguity by explicitly overriding the method.

checkpoint.question: What is a Functional Interface in Java?
options: An interface that contains exactly one abstract method (annotated with @FunctionalInterface), enabling it to be implemented using lambda expressions
An interface with no methods at all
An interface that only contains static methods
An interface used exclusively for mathematical operations
checkpoint.explanation: A Functional Interface (like Runnable, Callable, Comparator) has exactly one abstract method (SAM: Single Abstract Method), allowing concise instantiation via lambda expressions or method references.

checkpoint.question: What is a Marker Interface in Java?
options: An interface with no fields or methods (e.g. Serializable, Cloneable) used to convey metadata or tag a class for special JVM/framework processing
An interface that highlights syntax errors in IDEs
An interface used exclusively for graphic drawing
An interface that can only be implemented once
checkpoint.explanation: Marker interfaces (like java.io.Serializable) have an empty body. They serve as a type marker, signaling to the JVM or frameworks that instances possess a specific capability.

checkpoint.question: What happens if a non-abstract (concrete) class extends an abstract class but fails to implement all of its abstract methods?
options: A compilation error occurs: the concrete class must either implement all inherited abstract methods or be declared abstract itself
The missing methods are filled with empty stubs by the JVM
The code compiles and throws an AbstractMethodError only if the method is called
The abstract methods are converted into private methods
checkpoint.explanation: A concrete class must provide implementations for all inherited abstract methods. If it does not, the class itself remains incomplete and must be declared abstract.

checkpoint.question: Why can't an abstract method in an abstract class be declared with 'private', 'static', or 'final' modifiers?
options: Because abstract methods exist to be overridden by subclasses; private prevents visibility, final prevents overriding, and static prevents dynamic dispatch
Because the JVM cannot store abstract keywords in bytecode
Because private methods run faster than abstract methods
Because static methods can only be written in interfaces
checkpoint.explanation: An abstract method MUST be overridden. 'private' would hide it from subclasses; 'final' explicitly forbids overriding; and 'static' means it belongs to the class and cannot be dynamically dispatched.

Always use Abstract Classes because Interfaces are slower

pages.title: Advantage of Upcasting
pages.content:
Upcasting stores a subclass object in a superclass reference. The code can then work with a general API while the concrete object remains specialized.

This supports flexible method calls and is a common foundation for runtime polymorphism.

checkpoint.question: What is upcasting in Java?
options: Treating a subclass object reference as a reference of its superclass or interface type (e.g. Animal a = new Dog())
Converting a primitive float to a double
Casting an object down to a more specific subclass using (Subclass)
Moving an object from the Heap to the Stack
checkpoint.explanation: Upcasting is narrowing the view of an object to its supertype (moving up the inheritance hierarchy). It is always safe and implicit in Java because a Dog IS-AN Animal.

checkpoint.question: Given: Animal a = new Dog(); Is an explicit cast (Animal) required in Java?
options: No, upcasting is performed implicitly by the Java compiler because an instance of a subclass is guaranteed to satisfy all superclass contracts
Yes, every cast in Java requires parentheses
Yes, unless both classes are in java.lang
No, but it causes a compiler warning
checkpoint.explanation: Upcasting is safe and implicit. The compiler allows assigning any subtype reference to a supertype reference variable without explicit cast operators.

pages.title: Upcasting Usage
pages.content:
Upcasting is implicit when a subclass object is assigned to a superclass reference. Only members visible through the superclass type can be accessed directly.

Overridden instance methods still dispatch to the subclass implementation at runtime.

checkpoint.question: What limitation is imposed when interacting with an object through an upcasted superclass reference (e.g. Shape s = new Circle())?
options: You can only directly access members declared in the Shape class (compile-time type); Circle-specific methods (like getRadius()) are not accessible without downcasting
The Circle object's fields are deleted from heap memory
The methods of Circle execute 50% slower
You cannot invoke any methods on 's'
checkpoint.explanation: The compiler restricts member access to what is declared in the reference type (Shape). Even though the underlying object is a Circle, methods unique to Circle cannot be called through reference s.

pages.title: Benefit of dynamic method dispatch
pages.content:
Dynamic method dispatch allows Java to choose an overridden instance method at runtime according to the actual object.

This makes code that depends on a parent type extensible: new subclasses can provide behavior without changing the caller.

checkpoint.question: What is Dynamic Method Dispatch in Java?
options: The runtime mechanism by which an invocation to an overridden instance method is resolved at runtime based on the actual object type rather than the reference type
A technique for compiling Java into native assembly code dynamically
A method for dispatching HTTP requests asynchronously
Executing methods in parallel across multi-core processors
checkpoint.explanation: Dynamic method dispatch is how Java achieves runtime polymorphism: when an overridden method is called on a reference, the JVM checks the actual object type on the heap and invokes its implementation.

pages.title: Dynamic Method Dispatch Behavior
pages.content:
When a parent reference points to a child object, an overridden instance method call uses the child implementation. This is runtime polymorphism.

The declared reference type still determines which methods the compiler allows the call site to access.
